patches.name: Deep Sub
patches.blurb: A sine two octaves down with everything above it filtered away. The note you feel rather than hear.

patches.name: Round Bass
patches.blurb: A sine sub with a triangle an octave above it, so the line still reads on a phone speaker.

patches.name: Acid Line
patches.blurb: Synth Voice with its filter envelope wide open, into a ladder for the squelch. Turn the ladder's resonance up.

patches.name: Rubber Pluck
patches.blurb: Short square with a resonant lowpass and a little clip on the way out. Bouncy rather than heavy.

patches.name: Reese
patches.blurb: Two saws a few cents apart, beating against each other. The detune is the whole sound.

patches.name: Growl Bass
patches.blurb: A saw ring modulated against a fixed low tone, then driven through a ladder. Metallic and rude.

patches.name: Wobble Bass
patches.blurb: An LFO on the ladder's cutoff, trimmed to 220 Hz to 2.6 kHz. Change the LFO rate and nothing else.

patches.name: Sub and Click
patches.blurb: A sine sub with a filtered noise transient on top, the noise opened by its own fast envelope.

patches.name: Square Lead
patches.blurb: A plain square through a lowpass and a short delay. The lead every other lead is a variation on.

patches.name: Dotted Saw
patches.blurb: Saw into a dotted eighth that locks to the host tempo. Play quarter notes and it fills itself in.

patches.name: Super Saw
patches.blurb: Synth Voice with unison most of the way up. Wide, and thin in the middle on purpose, so a bass fits under it.

patches.name: Hollow Pulse
patches.blurb: A narrow pulse with a slow LFO on its width. The classic hollow-to-full sweep, and it is one cable.

patches.name: Ring Lead
patches.blurb: A triangle multiplied by a sine an octave and a quarter tone above it, both played by the keys. Inharmonic, and it still follows the melody.

patches.name: Octave Lead
patches.blurb: Two squares an octave apart, the upper one quiet. Doubles a melody without anybody playing two parts.

patches.name: Chorused Lead
patches.blurb: A short modulated delay mixed half in, which is all a chorus is. The LFO is on the delay time.

patches.name: Gritty Lead
patches.blurb: Saw into a wavefolder at two thirds wet. Folding adds harmonics a filter cannot put back.

patches.name: Warm Pad
patches.blurb: Slow saw, filter well down, reverb behind it. The bed everything else sits on.

patches.name: Glass Pad
patches.blurb: A wavetable with the low end taken out and a long delay after it. Bright without being sharp.

patches.name: Breathing Pad
patches.blurb: One slow LFO on the filter, trimmed to 500 Hz to 4 kHz. Nothing else moves, and that is the point.

patches.name: String Machine
patches.blurb: Two detuned saws through a chorus, which is a twenty millisecond delay with an LFO on its time.

patches.name: Choir Pad
patches.blurb: A harmonic oscillator through two narrow bandpasses at 520 and 1500 Hz. Two fixed formants, and it reads as a voice.

patches.name: Dark Drone
patches.blurb: A triangle an octave down with a sine under it, filtered to almost nothing and left to ring.

patches.name: Shimmer Pad
patches.blurb: The dry pad and a copy of it an octave up both feed the reverb. The octave never reaches the output on its own.

patches.name: Slow Swell
patches.blurb: Almost two seconds of attack and four of release. Hold a chord, let go, and it is still going.

patches.name: Electric Piano
patches.blurb: A sine with a quiet triangle an octave up, a short ping two octaves up for the tine, and a tempo locked tremolo on the end.

patches.name: Bell
patches.blurb: A sine multiplied by a second sine just under two octaves above it, both played by the keys. The partials land between the harmonics, which is what makes a bell a bell.

patches.name: Marimba
patches.blurb: A short sine with a shorter sine an octave above it. Wooden because the top one dies first.

patches.name: Nylon Pluck
patches.blurb: A variable shape oscillator with a soft filter and a small room. Close to a nylon string if you play it gently.

patches.name: Clav
patches.blurb: A narrow pulse through a resonant bandpass and a little clip. All attack, no tail.

patches.name: Music Box
patches.blurb: Two sines two octaves apart, pitched an octave up where a music box plays, both decaying to nothing in a fairly wet room.

patches.name: Harpsichord
patches.blurb: Saw plus a square an octave up, the bottom filtered off. Thin on purpose.

patches.name: Toy Piano
patches.blurb: Triangle and square, both an octave or two up, squeezed through a bandpass. Small and slightly wrong.

patches.name: Kick
patches.blurb: A sine body two octaves down, a short triangle for the knock, and a higher triangle for the beater. Play the note that matches the kit.

patches.name: Snare
patches.blurb: Filtered noise for the wires and a 190 Hz tone for the drum, each with its own envelope.

patches.name: Hi-Hat
patches.blurb: White noise above 8 kHz with a closed-hat envelope. Lengthen the decay and it is an open hat.

patches.name: Tom
patches.blurb: The kick's three voices, one octave up and held longer. Knock is the skin. Play the note that matches the drum.

patches.name: Clap
patches.blurb: Noise through a wide bandpass with a slower decay than a hat, and a small room to smear it.

patches.name: Rimshot
patches.blurb: A very narrow bandpass on noise plus a 400 Hz click. Almost no decay at all.

patches.name: Euclid Bass
patches.blurb: Seven hits in sixteen steps, which is a pattern rather than a faster clock. The sequencer follows the same hits.

patches.name: Acid Sequence
patches.blurb: Sixteenths through a Synth Voice and a ladder. The melody is eight numbers in the sequencer, so change them.

patches.name: Random Bleeps
patches.blurb: A stepped random into a quantizer, so the notes are random and in key. Change the quantizer's root and scale.

patches.name: Slow Arp
patches.blurb: An eight step arpeggio on a wavetable with a dotted delay behind it. Eighth notes, so it sits under something.

patches.name: Techno Pulse
patches.blurb: A quarter note kick and an eighth note hat, each from its own clock. The kick's pitch drop is an envelope on a tone.

patches.name: Ambient Bloom
patches.blurb: One note a bar, a second of attack on each, and a big room. Leave it running.

patches.name: Krell
patches.blurb: A random voltage sets the clock rate, so the rhythm never settles. The classic self playing patch.

patches.name: Poly Clock
patches.blurb: One clock divided by three against the same clock multiplied by two. Two voices that agree once a bar and nowhere else.

patches.name: Drone Field
patches.blurb: Two held notes from two Control nodes, each breathing at its own rate. No clock anywhere in it.

patches.name: Noise Rain
patches.blurb: Nine hits in sixteen steps on filtered noise, with a random voltage moving the filter. Percussion with no drums in it.

patches.name: Telephone
patches.blurb: Everything outside 400 Hz to 2.6 kHz taken away, with a little clip for the cheap speaker.

patches.name: Lo-fi Radio
patches.blurb: A band around the middle, then asymmetric shaping. Thin and slightly broken, which is the whole idea.

patches.name: Tilt EQ
patches.blurb: A shelf up at the bottom and the same shelf down at the top. One move, two bands, and it stays balanced.

patches.name: Auto Wah
patches.blurb: An envelope follower on the ladder's cutoff, so the filter opens as hard as you play. Trimmed so it rests near 300 Hz and an ordinary strum opens it past 2 kHz.

patches.name: Filter Sweep
patches.blurb: A five second LFO on a state variable filter. Slow enough to be a build rather than a wobble.

patches.name: Sub Boost
patches.blurb: Six decibels under 90 Hz with a limiter behind it, because that is six decibels of headroom gone.

patches.name: Air Lift
patches.blurb: A wide shelf at 9 kHz and a small cut at 250, which is the oldest trick for making something sound expensive.

patches.name: Formant
patches.blurb: Two narrow bandpasses in parallel at 700 and 1150 Hz, summed. Those two numbers are roughly where a spoken vowel sits.

patches.name: Warm Saturation
patches.blurb: Asymmetric shaping at four fifths wet, then a shelf to put the weight back. Tape flattery, roughly.

patches.name: Fuzz
patches.blurb: Hard clipping at eight times, with the top rolled off so it is rude rather than painful.

patches.name: Bitcrusher
patches.blurb: Six bits, with a lowpass after it to take the worst of the aliasing off.

patches.name: Rate Crush
patches.blurb: Every eighth sample held. Different from bit crushing: this one takes the top away rather than the detail.

patches.name: Wavefolder
patches.blurb: Folding rather than clipping, so it adds harmonics a filter cannot put back. Loud input folds more.

patches.name: Tape Drive
patches.blurb: Soft clip, bass shelf up, treble shelf down. Three moves, and together they are a tape machine.

patches.name: Octave Fuzz
patches.blurb: Full rectification doubles the frequency before the clipping stage. The octave is free.

patches.name: Ring Mod
patches.blurb: Multiplied by a fixed 140 Hz. Not in key with anything, which is what it is for.

patches.name: Slapback
patches.blurb: One repeat at 110 milliseconds. Short enough to read as a room rather than an echo.

patches.name: Tape Echo
patches.blurb: Quarter notes locked to the host, with the repeats filtered. Each one comes back darker than the last.

patches.name: Dotted Eighth
patches.blurb: The delay that fills a bar without landing on the beat. Play quarter notes over it.

patches.name: Dub Delay
patches.blurb: High feedback with the repeats banded between 200 Hz and 1.8 kHz, so they decay into mud rather than into hiss.

patches.name: Reverse Delay
patches.blurb: Half second buffers played backwards, then delayed. Swells that arrive before the note does.

patches.name: Octave Delay
patches.blurb: The dry signal and a copy an octave down both go into the delay. Only the repeats are pitched.

patches.name: Stutter
patches.blurb: A sixteenth note tremolo chopping the signal, then a sixteenth note delay catching the pieces.

patches.name: Triplet Echo
patches.blurb: Eighth note triplets. Against a straight part it is the cheapest way to make a bar feel busy.

patches.name: Small Room
patches.blurb: Barely there. Enough to stop something sounding like it was recorded in a box.

patches.name: Big Hall
patches.blurb: Long and dark. Put it after something that has already stopped playing.

patches.name: Plate
patches.blurb: Short, bright and dense, with a shelf on top. The reverb for a snare.

patches.name: Shimmer
patches.blurb: An octave up feeding the same reverb as the dry signal. The pitch shifter never reaches the output on its own.

patches.name: Gated Reverb
patches.blurb: A big reverb with a gate across it, so the tail stops dead. The sound of 1984, and it is two modules.

patches.name: Dark Cavern
patches.blurb: Damping right down and a lowpass after it. Nothing above 2 kHz survives the trip.

patches.name: Ambient Wash
patches.blurb: A half note delay into a long reverb. The order matters: reverb into delay is a different, muddier patch.

patches.name: Chorus
patches.blurb: A twenty millisecond delay with an LFO on its time, mixed half in. That is all a chorus has ever been.

patches.name: Flanger
patches.blurb: A comb filter with an LFO on its frequency and the feedback well up. Jet plane territory.

patches.name: Phaser
patches.blurb: Two allpass stages swept by one LFO, summed back with the dry signal. Allpass changes phase and not level, so the notches are where the two cancel, and that is the sweep.

patches.name: Tremolo
patches.blurb: Eighth notes, locked to the host. Depth at 0.6 so it breathes rather than chops.

patches.name: Auto Pan
patches.blurb: Side to side just under once a second. On headphones this is a lot; on speakers it is barely there.

patches.name: Vibrato
patches.blurb: The chorus with no dry signal in it. An eight millisecond delay, fully wet, with the LFO on its time.

patches.name: Rotary
patches.blurb: Fast panning with the filter moving in step, because a rotating speaker gets darker as it turns away.

patches.name: Sample and Hold
patches.blurb: A stepped random on the cutoff, seven steps a second. Held values, not a sweep, which is the difference that matters.

patches.name: Vocal Comp
patches.blurb: Four to one with a fast attack and makeup to bring it back. The one that makes a take sit still.

patches.name: Drum Glue
patches.blurb: Gentle ratio, slow attack so the transients get through, release timed to let it breathe between hits.

patches.name: Brickwall
patches.blurb: A ceiling and nothing else. Put it last, and if it is working hard, turn something else down.

patches.name: Noise Gate
patches.blurb: Closes below three percent, with a hold so it does not chatter on a decaying note.

patches.name: Punch
patches.blurb: Transient shaping: attack up, sustain down. It finds the hits by itself, so there is no threshold to set.

patches.name: Parallel Comp
patches.blurb: A heavily squashed copy summed back with the dry. Both cables land on the same inlet, which is how crate mixes.

patches.name: Pump
patches.blurb: A quarter note clock, widened by a pulse, into the ducker's sidechain. Sidechain pumping with nothing to sidechain from.

patches.name: Widener
patches.blurb: Side signal up by half. Check it in mono afterwards: width is borrowed from the centre.

patches.name: Haas Spread
patches.blurb: One side delayed by sixteen milliseconds. Under about thirty the ear hears position rather than an echo.

patches.name: Mono Below
patches.blurb: Under 180 Hz folded to mono, above it widened. The high band is inverted so the two halves sum flat across the crossover. The standard treatment for a bass that will be cut to vinyl.

patches.name: Mid Side Lift
patches.blurb: Encode, shelve the top, decode. Between those two nodes the left channel is the middle and the right is the sides.

patches.name: Stereo Flip
patches.blurb: Left becomes right. One module, and it is the fastest way to find out whether a part was panned by accident.

patches.name: Slow Panner
patches.blurb: Once every seven seconds, almost the full width. Slow enough that nobody notices it and the mix moves anyway.
